candidates.title: Delusion-like content emerges from common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations
candidates.abstract: Delusions are beliefs with extraordinary content, yet computational accounts of delusions have not explained how this content arises. We propose that extraordinary content emerges when an ordinary mechanism, common-cause inference, is applied to semantically disparate observations. We tested this with large language models (LLMs) by systematically manipulating semantic disparity between observations. Single causes inferred by these models from ordinary observations generally resembled true causes, yet became increasingly delusion-like as observations became more disparate. Observation disparity predicted delusionality, and this relationship could be explained geometrically via semantic analogues of common-cause properties. We further tested this idea in a large corpus of real-world delusions. In cases documenting pre-delusional observations, subsequent delusional beliefs were consistent with what LLMs would infer and exhibited corresponding common-cause properties. Together, our findings identify a computational route through which extraordinary delusion-like content can emerge from ordinary causal inference, and demonstrate its relevance to clinical delusions.

candidates.title: Artificial intelligence and clinical reasoning - a qualitative study with general practice trainees in Germany
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background General practitioners face high complexity in clinical decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) may support clinical reasoning, but their impact on decision-making processes and postgraduate medical training remains unclear. This qualitative study aims to explore General Practice (GP) trainee’s use of LLMs in clinical reasoning and their educational needs. Materials and methods GP trainees were recruited and interviewed with semi-structured interview-guide. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed qualitatively. Results Seventeen GP trainees participated (mean interview duration: 38 min; range: 21–63 min). AI was perceived as a tool to augment and accelerate clinical decision-making, while potential risks of deskilling were identified. Participants reported a lack of structured AI education and expressed a need for its integration into postgraduate training. Discussion Participants perceived AI primarily as a supportive tool that can complement clinical reasoning and improve access to medical knowledge. At the same time, they identified potential risks, including overreliance on AI-generated information and possible effects on the development of clinical expertise. These findings suggest that postgraduate medical training should address AI-related competencies, including critical appraisal, ethical responsibility and appropriate integration of AI into clinical decision-making. Conclusion AI is already part of clinical practice among GP trainees, offering opportunities to support learning and clinical reasoning while raising concerns about overreliance and critical appraisal. Postgraduate medical training in GP should therefore incorporate structured AI competencies to ensure responsible, reflective and patient-centered use of AI.

candidates.title: Effects of a Personalized Retrieval-Augmented Generation Chatbot on Information Needs in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease: Mixed Methods Randomized Controlled Trial
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Patients receiving dialysis for chronic kidney disease encounter complex self-management challenges and ongoing information needs that traditional health care often fails to meet. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances the factual accuracy of large language models (LLMs), but whether personalized RAG is more effective than general RAG remains unclear. Objective This study aimed to assess whether personalized constraint retrieval-augmented generation (C-RAG) is more effective than open-domain general retrieval-augmented generation (O-RAG) and standard care in reducing information needs among patients receiving dialysis and to identify predictors of chatbot engagement. Methods A sequential 2-phase mixed methods study was conducted. Phase 1 evaluated 4 LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Anthropic], Gemini 1.5 Flash [Google], CLOVA X [NAVER], and ChatGPT-4o [OpenAI]) using 60 patient-generated questions, assessed by 15 clinical experts. Phase 2 was a 3-arm parallel pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT; October-December 2025) at 3 tertiary hospitals in South Korea. Based on phase 1 findings, 2 chatbot variants were developed using GPT-4o—C-RAG, which incorporates patient-specific clinical parameters, and O-RAG, which uses the same knowledge base without personalization. Participants were randomized 1:1:1 to C-RAG, O-RAG, or standard care. The primary outcome, change in medication, dietary, and diagnostic information needs (5-point Likert scales) from baseline to 4 weeks, was analyzed using ANCOVA. Semistructured interviews with 9 participants explored underlying mechanisms. Results ChatGPT-4o achieved the highest scores in clinical accuracy (mean 3.60, SD 0.95), safety (mean 3.67, SD 1.00), and readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level 9.8, compared with 13.2‐14.5 for other models). In phase 2, 42/45 (93%) enrolled participants completed the study (14 per group). ANCOVA revealed significant group differences in medication ( F 2,38 =4.574, P =.02) and dietary ( F 2,38 =4.232, P =.02) information needs. In Bonferroni-corrected comparisons, C-RAG had lower needs than O-RAG in both domains (observed mean 2.93, SD 1.21 vs mean 3.86, SD 0.95; Cohen d =−0.86, 95% CI −1.63 to −0.08; P =.02 for both). Against control, C-RAG showed medium-to-large but nonsignificant effects (medication Cohen d =−0.64, 95% CI −1.39 to 0.12; dietary Cohen d =−0.54, 95% CI −1.30 to 0.21). Secondary outcomes did not differ between groups. Dietary management emerged as the most frequent query topic, accounting for 29.3% (205/691) of total queries. Participants on dialysis for 1‐3 years showed higher engagement (9/10, 90% engagement for 1‐3 y vs 5/18, 27.8% for ≥4 y; Fisher exact P =.006). Qualitative analysis revealed 5 themes, including dietary management as the primary need and dialysis duration as a moderator of utility. Conclusions In this pilot trial, personalized RAG showed lower information needs than general RAG, with a large effect size (Cohen d =−0.86). The medium-to-large effects against standard care (Cohen d =−0.54 to −0.64) support a fully powered confirmatory trial (estimated 50‐55 participants per group) to evaluate long-term clinical outcomes.

candidates.title: Retrieval augmented consistency scoring for model agnostic hallucination detection in large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, education, and scientific research, where factual accuracy is paramount. However, LLMs frequently generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect statements, a phenomenon widely known as hallucination. Existing detection approaches are constrained by significant practical limitations: white-box methods require access to model internals that are inaccessible from commercial APIs; self-consistency sampling incurs prohibitive inference overhead ($k\times$ additional LLM calls); and perplexity-based signals fail to distinguish factual errors from genuinely novel correct statements. In this paper, we propose RAG-CS (Retrieval-Augmented Consistency Scoring), a post-hoc, model-agnostic hallucination detection framework requiring no access to LLM logits, weights, or sampling distributions. Given any LLM-generated response, RAG-CS first sentence-segments the output, then retrieves the top-$k$ evidence passages per sentence from a knowledge corpus using a dense bi-encoder retriever indexed with FAISS. A cross-encoder natural language inference (NLI) model computes pairwise semantic consistency scores between each response sentence and its retrieved evidence. Finally, a lightweight logistic regression classifier aggregates these scores, including statistical features over the score distribution, into a binary hallucination label and per-sentence fine-grained indicators. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on four hallucination benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HaluEval, FEVER, and FaithDial) and demonstrate that RAG-CS achieves F1 scores of 87.3\%, 84.6\%, 89.1\%, and 83.7\%, respectively, outperforming strong baselines including SelfCheckGPT-NLI, SAPLMA, and FActScore by 4.1--9.8 percentage points. Crucially, RAG-CS generalizes across generating models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA-2-7B/13B, Mistral-7B) with no model-specific tuning, and requires only a single LLM inference call plus under 300~ms of retrieval and scoring overhead per query. Ablation studies rigorously confirm the complementary, indispensable contributions of dense retrieval and cross-encoder NLI scoring. Qualitative analysis reveals interpretable per-sentence hallucination patterns. We release all code, retrieval indices, and model checkpoints to support reproducible research.

candidates.title: FaithChart: Measuring and Improving the Visual Grounding of Chart Explanations in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now exceed 90% accuracy on chart question answering, yet whether their explanations are causally grounded in the visual evidence they cite remains unmeasured. We introduce FaithChart, a framework that measures and improves the visual grounding of chart explanations. First, we propose two causal, black-box metrics—Sufficiency and Comprehensiveness—computed by perturbing cited chart-image regions and observing the change in predictions. Second, we release FaithChart-1500, a benchmark of 1,498 human-verified samples with dual-LLM reasoning traces. Third, we introduce FaithChart-B, a parameter-efficient model whose structured evidence supervision cuts the sufficiency–comprehensiveness imbalance by 88% at only a 5.5-point accuracy cost. Across four state-of-the-art MLLMs, faithfulness ranking inverts accuracy ranking—the most accurate model is not the most faithful, and correctness does not predict grounding. FaithChart offers a reproducible instrument for auditing and training visually grounded multimodal reasoning.

candidates.title: Continuous-Space Diffusion and Flow Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Continuous-space diffusion and flow language models generate text by updating real-valued vectors (such as token embeddings, compressed codes, or sentence vectors) and decoding them into discrete words at readout. We organize this literature by three coupled choices: the continuous state being refined, the transition operator that updates it, and the text interface that converts states into tokens. Because language is discrete while the state space is continuous, adapting image diffusion to text encounters rounding ambiguity and embedding collapse under squared-error regression, uninformative noise schedules, distribution shift between clean-text codecs and learned priors, and mode averaging in few-step sampling. Across published comparisons with autoregressive and discrete-diffusion baselines, continuous models show no general advantage over same-scale autoregressive models on open-ended text; the closest prompt-continuation tie uses different training sequence lengths and separately tuned samplers. RePlaid matches or improves upon masked diffusion in likelihood bounds past compute-optimal budgets, and large-scale blockwise adaptation brings continuous models close to masked baselines on mathematical reasoning and code; however, continuous models still trail autoregressive baselines in held-out likelihood bounds, and scaling fits indicate that matching exact autoregressive negative log-likelihood requires substantially more training compute. Their clearest gains over autoregressive decoding appear in gradient-guided control, plan-level diversity, and task-specific reasoning after targeted fine-tuning. Under few-step budgets, trajectory-consistent distillation and stochastic bridges prevent entropy collapse, yet no standalone continuous generator has shown an end-to-end latency win over optimized autoregressive decoding at matched quality; the reported matched-quality latency gains rely on autoregressive verification of continuous drafts. We close with open problems in likelihood scaling, readout fidelity, few-step serving, representation reuse, and post-training.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Enhancing LLMs with External Knowledge
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) generate fluent answers, but they depend mainly on their training data. As a result they can give wrong or outdated responses, and they may lack the specific information a question needs. Retraining a model again and again to fix this takes a great deal of time. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses the problem by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources, such as documents, databases and the web, before a response is generated. This paper presents a literature survey and problem understanding for RAG. It explains the retrieve–augment–generate workflow, states the problem and six objectives, and relates RAG to current technology trends: real-time information, enterprise AI, agentic AI, cost-effective scalability and reduced hallucination. Eight studies from 2020 to 2026 are compared on methodology, key findings and limitations. The analysis reveals that the quality of information retrieval, as well as the effectiveness, accuracy and assessment, still remain unstudied topics. Four research gaps are identified: high computational resources, irrelevant or incomplete retrieval, limited effectiveness in specialised domains, and the need for better evaluation of factuality, relevance and reliability.

candidates.title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

candidates.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

candidates.title: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation for domain knowledge enhancement in large language models
candidates.abstract: Large language models are susceptible to problems such as lagging parameter knowledge updates, insufficient alignment of textual and graphical evidence, and incomplete factual basis for answers in domain-specific question answering. To address these issues, a domain-consistent multimodal retrieval enhancement generation framework, DC-MRAG, is proposed. This framework comprises four modules: domain anchor index, hierarchical cross-modal retrieval, evidence consistency fusion, and uncertainty-aware generation. It achieves unified representation of textual and graphical evidence through domain concept constraints, utilizes multi-factor scoring for candidate recall and re-ranking, compresses context based on evidence support, and controls generation risk through confidence calibration and selective secondary retrieval. Under a unified example experimental setting, the proposed method achieves an exact match rate of 84.9%, a recall@5 rate of 91.4%, an answer fidelity of 94.2%, and a phantom rate reduction to 4.6%. Compared to RAMQA, the exact match rate is improved by 4.2 percentage points, the phantom rate is relatively reduced by 41.03%, context tokens are reduced by 26.99%, P95 response latency is reduced by 23.43%, and throughput is increased by 28.85%. The results show that the collaborative design of domain indexing, cross-modal retrieval, evidence fusion, and generative calibration can improve the accuracy, evidence reliability, and online service efficiency of knowledge-based question answering.

candidates.title: InceptionRAG: Stealthy Poisoning Attack Against Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge but have been demonstrated to be vulnerable to corpus poisoning. Existing poisoning attacks against RAG largely focus on single-point explicit injection, where the malicious payload is fully encapsulated within a single document. Consequently, recent mitigation mechanisms have evolved to identify and diminish these threats effectively. In this paper, we first verify that existing mitigation mechanisms are insufficient for a new class of threats: indirect logic induction. Motivated by this observation, we introduce InceptionRAG, a stealthy attack mechanism that subverts the standard attack paradigm. Instead of injecting explicit malicious payloads, InceptionRAG fragments it into a chain of dormant passages. These passages appear harmless and can bypass existing mitigation mechanisms when examined separately. However, when retrieved together, they trigger LLMs to self-deduce target misinformation via multi-hop reasoning. To further improve the applicability of InceptionRAG in black-box settings, we propose zeroth-order suffix optimization (ZOSO) to automate the generation of authoritative suffixes. Extensive evaluations across three datasets and three LLMs demonstrate that InceptionRAG achieves an attack success rate exceeding 80% even under rigorous adversarial constraints. In particular, InceptionRAG shows superior evasion capabilities, effectively bypassing established defenses that mitigate traditional single-document injections. Our findings expose a concerning paradox: the stronger reasoning capabilities of LLMs increase their vulnerability to reasoning-based poisoning attacks. To mitigate potential misuse, we propose a document isolation-based defense, HODOR, which decouples adversarial logical dependencies.

candidates.title: FPSRG: Heterogeneous User Simulation First-Person Post-Training and Multidimensional Semantic Response Grids
candidates.abstract: Simulating heterogeneous individuals with large language models is an active research direction, and heterogeneous user simulation requires models with different characteristics. We study profile construction: given dimensions, items, and scoring rules, build model configurations that can be retrieved by multidimensional target scores. We introduce First-Person Semantic Response Grids (FPSRG). Shared post-training first teaches the model to judge and answer as the participant; self-report and behavioral targets then refine dimension-specific control vectors. With the model frozen, we measure joint scores for vector-coefficient combinations, filter inadmissible configurations, and store the results in a searchable catalog. Per-token configuration routing, continuous batching, and isolated caches support parallel measurement of different profiles. Non-thinking five- and ten-dimensional Qwen instances and a thinking-mode six-dimensional instance following full-parameter post-training of Huihui demonstrate the complete workflow. With matched data, layers, and norms, refinement increases mean five-axis composite control span from 30.75 to 40.45. Within the five-dimensional 25-75 target region, the qualified five-level vector catalog covers 92.2% of fixed targets under per-axis error at most 20 and total error at most 60; combining it with the prompt catalog increases coverage to 98.7%. At a fixed coefficient range, three-, five-, and nine-level catalogs achieve 71.2%, 92.2%, and 94.6% coverage, demonstrating the gains from denser measurement. These results describe measured reachable regions under a fixed assessment protocol. Through shared adaptation, a small set of learned directions, and reusable joint measurements, FPSRG constructs heterogeneous individual configurations without retraining a model for every profile.

candidates.title: Enhancing capability boundaries of in-context learning in large language models for computer vision
candidates.abstract: Visual context learning enables large language models to perform visual question answering and cross-scene reasoning based on a limited number of image and text examples. However, its performance is limited by factors such as example redundancy, visual token overhead, insufficient cross-modal alignment, and prediction confidence bias. To address these issues, this paper proposes a boundary-enhanced visual context learning framework, BEV-ICL. It improves the task relevance and structural diversity of examples through boundary-aware example selection and rearrangement, preserves key objects and spatial relationships using structure-aware visual token compression, achieves dynamic alignment of visual evidence with question semantics through relational conditional gating, and enhances output reliability through uncertainty-aware reasoning and probability calibration. In the constructed experimental scheme, the average accuracy of the proposed method reached 69.6%, an improvement of 4.4 percentage points compared to the comparison method. The long context accuracy increased from 57.3% to 68.9%; the number of context tokens decreased from 5120 to 3200, a reduction of 37.50%; the average inference latency decreased from 428.6 ms to 286.4 ms , a reduction of 33.18%; P95 latency decreased by 34.29%; system throughput increased from 22.4 req/s to 33.8 req/s, an increase of 50.89%; and the expected calibration error decreased from 6.8% to 4.1%. These results demonstrate that jointly optimizing example configuration, visual structure compression, cross-modal relationships, and prediction calibration can expand the applicability of visual context learning in terms of task performance, context capacity, and inference efficiency.

candidates.title: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, offering a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language modeling. However, each denoising step requires a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length, and a fixed step budget further compounds this quadratic per-step cost. Existing inference acceleration approaches for multimodal dLLMs characterize attention redundancy implicitly, motivating designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. We close this gap with DRAMA, a training-free acceleration framework grounded in a systematic dissection of attention redundancy in multimodal dLLMs. By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, we reveal two persistent redundancy structures: (i) attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and (ii) attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms: Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS). Together, DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Our results establish a strong, measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal dLLM inference.

candidates.title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
candidates.abstract: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.

candidates.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
candidates.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

candidates.title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

candidates.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Chatbot for Academic Information Services Using GROQ API
candidates.abstract: Academic information services in universities are still largely carried out manually by administrative staff with limited working hours, making it difficult for students to receive quick responses, especially outside office hours. This study aims to design and implement an academic chatbot using the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach through the Groq API and a Streamlit interface. The system was developed following the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology, which includes problem identification, defining solution objectives, dataset collection, artifact design and development, system demonstration, testing and evaluation, as well as communication of research results. Black-box testing on 20 questions yielded 18 valid answers, while semantic quality evaluation using BERTScore produced a precision of 0.7054, recall of 0.7176, and F1-score of 0.7095. The average system response time was 1.45 seconds, with a median of 0.85 seconds, indicates that the majority of responses were provided in less than one second, despite a single outlier of 12.13 seconds. These results finding suggest that the integration of RAG with the Groq API holds potential for enhancing digital academic information services in higher education. Nevertheless, its operational benefits in real-world scenarios warrant further evaluation through empirical user testing.

candidates.title: RMIT-ADM+S at TREC RAG 2026: Research Agents, Retriever Ablations, and Open-Weight Replication
candidates.abstract: We describe the RMIT-ADM+S team's participation in the TREC 2026 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) track using the ClimbMix corpus. We submitted seven research-agent runs using proprietary OpenAI and open-weight models, exploring different retrieval strategies, writer models, and agent workflows. Pre-submission ablations identified writer selection and adjacent-chunk expansion as the main factors affecting answer quality. In the official NIST evaluation, six of seven runs exceeded the track median across all three rubric/nugget collections. Our best-performing run, brief-hybrid, achieved the highest all-item coverage among our submissions and tied the track maximum (0.892) for Batch-1 vital coverage. Human side-by-side preferences differed across evaluation batches: the open-weight owa-glm5 led Batch 1 despite lower automated coverage, while sol-research-first led Batch 2. These findings highlight differences between automated coverage measures and human preferences, as well as the potential of lower-cost open-weight models for research-agent systems.

candidates.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

candidates.title: Large language models for mental health
candidates.abstract: Digital technologies have long been explored as a complement to standard procedure in mental health research and practice, ranging from the management of electronic health records to app-based interventions. The recent emergence of large language models (LLMs), both proprietary and open-source ones, represents a major new opportunity on that front. Yet there is still a divide between the community developing LLMs and the one which may benefit from them, thus hindering the beneficial translation of the technology into clinical use. This divide largely stems from the lack of a common language and understanding regarding the technology’s inner workings, capabilities, and risks. Our tutorial-style review attempts to bridge this gap by providing intuitive explanations behind the basic concepts related to contemporary LLMs.

candidates.title: Large Language Models as Digital Twins: a Distribution-Aware Questionnaire-Based Evaluation
candidates.abstract: This paper investigates whether Large Language Models can answer a personality questionnaire as a specific individual would. Given a user's social-media posts, the model completes the BFI-2-60 Big Five questionnaire as that user. The predicted responses are converted into trait scores and compared with the user's actual scores. We evaluate GPT-4, Gemma, Llama 3.1, and Mistral on the MyPersonality dataset. To determine whether predictions reflect information from the user's writing, we compare them with answers produced without user text and with values derived from general population tendencies. We measure prediction error across all users and separately for individuals with low, intermediate, and high trait scores. We also test whether an LLM can express an explicit personality profile when given only the target Big Five scores, without user text, and examine how predictions change as more text is provided. The results show that user text does not consistently improve performance. Models perform better near the middle of the trait distribution, while at the lower and upper ends they often remain close to central values or perform well at one end but poorly at the other. When given an explicit profile, GPT-4 most clearly translates trait information into consistent questionnaire responses, particularly for Extraversion and Neuroticism. Increasing context does not systematically reduce error: open-source models fluctuate more, whereas GPT-4 remains comparatively stable. Overall, the evaluated models do not consistently reproduce the questionnaire behavior of specific individuals.

candidates.title: Hyperbolic Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract. Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success and demonstrated superior performance across various tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), weather forecasting, biological protein folding, text generation, and solving mathematical problems. However, many real-world data exhibit highly non-Euclidean latent hierarchical anatomy, such as protein networks, transportation networks, financial networks, brain networks, and linguistic structures or syntactic trees in natural languages. Effectively learning intrinsic semantic entailment and hierarchical relationships from these raw, unstructured input data using LLMs remains an underexplored area. Due to its effectiveness in modeling tree-like hierarchical structures, hyperbolic geometry—a non-Euclidean space—has rapidly gained popularity as an expressive latent representation space for complex data modeling across domains such as graphs, images, languages, and multimodal data. Here, we provide a comprehensive and contextual exposition of recent advancements in LLMs that leverage hyperbolic geometry as a representation space to enhance semantic representation learning and multiscale reasoning. Specifically, the paper presents a taxonomy of the principal techniques of hyperbolic LLMs (HypLLMs) in terms of four main categories: (1) hyperbolic LLMs through exp/log maps; (2) hyperbolic fine-tuned models; (3) fully hyperbolic LLMs; and (4) hyperbolic state-space models. We also explore crucial potential applications and outline future research directions. A repository of key papers, models, datasets, and code implementations is available at https://github.com/sarangp2402/Hyperbolic-LLM-Models .

candidates.title: From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation
candidates.abstract: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.

candidates.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
candidates.abstract: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

candidates.title: CURATOR: Scalable Fine-grained Evidence Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Decision Models
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides entire retrieved passages to the LLM, even though only a handful of spans within them contain the evidence pertaining to the question. While precise selection of these spans can improve context utilization, identifying them in isolation is challenging. A span may appear irrelevant by itself, and deciding whether to retain it may require examining other retrieved information. One can evaluate each span's candidacy with the full retrieved context, but this is computationally inefficient as the same text must be processed repeatedly. Pretrained decision model can be used to efficiently evaluate multiple spans simultaneously, allowing each decision to consider the surrounding spans as well. However, our experiments show that their ability to identify relevant evidence deteriorates as the number of simultaneous decisions increases. To address this, we introduce CURATOR, a fine-tuned decision model trained to make reliable evidence-selection decisions over large candidate sets. By training a decision model to select varying numbers of supporting spans from large candidate pools, CURATOR develops the capability to select evidence for RAG while retaining the computational efficiency of joint decision-making. We observe that CURATOR maintains a strong evidence discrimination capability as the number of candidates increases, generalizes across different tasks and document domains, and improves downstream RAG performance, particularly when the available context is limited.

candidates.title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts

candidates.title: <scp>MMAligner:</scp> Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often refuse unsafe text prompts yet generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses either rely on external guardrails, which add inference overhead without repairing intrinsic flaws, or safety fine-tuning, which treats alignment as black-box optimization and may sacrifice utility or require large multimodal datasets. To identify the cause of this safety disparity, we analyze MLLM representations geometrically. We find that safety mechanisms learned from text persist across modalities: a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary remain effective, and representations inside this boundary consistently trigger refusals. However, unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places most of them outside the boundary, allowing them to bypass the model's intrinsic safety mechanism. This indicates that multimodal safety degradation stems from representation misalignment rather than the absence of safety capability. Based on this finding, we propose MMAligner, a safeguarding method that calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the pre-existing refusal region. MMAligner applies a hard lower bound to ensure refusal, a soft upper bound to avoid excessive modification, and a preservation objective for benign inputs. Experiments across multiple open-source MLLMs show that MMAligner raises the average refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data, substantially improving the safety-utility trade-off over existing baselines. candidates.title: StateAlign: Internalizing State-Aware Decision-Making for Reliable Multi-Turn Tool Agents via Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning has improved the tool-use capabilities of large language models. However, better task performance can coincide with increased tool hallucination. Reliable tool use requires decisions to follow the current task state: available information, tool capabilities, and task progress. Our analysis shows that agents sometimes execute when they should ask for information, retrieve it, or decline an infeasible request, even when reasoning identifies missing information. We introduce StateAlign, combining task-state construction with state-contrastive reinforcement learning. The data cover five task conditions and pair states with different action requirements. Outcome rewards guide task completion; token-level contrasts compare the same generated reasoning and actions under paired states to train outputs that fit the current state. Experiments across five base models from three families show improvements on BFCL v4 multi-turn, ToolSandbox, and When2Call. Ablations show that state construction improves performance and reliability under different reward designs. The complete method further reduces tool hallucination across three Qwen3 sizes. On Qwen3-8B, StateAlign improves BFCL v4 multi-turn accuracy from 45.5% to 55.2% and reduces no-tool hallucination on SimpleToolHalluBench from 62.2% under outcome-only training to 56.1%. Behavioral analyses show more consistent decisions, more complete multi-call execution, and stronger recovery after tool errors.

candidates.title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression
candidates.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.

candidates.title: Active Learning of Approximate LLM Ranking for Energy-Efficient Retrieval of Long Queries
candidates.abstract: Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer complementary strengths for document retrieval: lexical retrievers which rely on keyword matching are fast and energy-efficient, whereas LLMs capture semantic meaning and excel at interpreting long, context-rich queries. However, this comes at a cost that is computationally and energetically prohibitive. We propose the LLM Active Approximation Model (LAAM), a hybrid retrieval framework that introduces a lightweight learned predictor which serves as an intermediary between semantic retrieval and LLM retrieval. LAAM is refined through an active learning loop where an LLM labels a small number of documents. By concentrating LLM evaluations on the most informative documents, the framework substantially reduces inference cost while preserving retrieval effectiveness. We evaluate the proposed framework on TREC Robust 2004 using Lucene with BM25 retrieval and DeepSeek v3 as the LLM, under three levels of query verbosity. For verbose queries, LAAM achieves 87% of average P@10 achieved by DeepSeek's reranking (0.459 vs. 0.526), while requiring only 3.3% of the per-query energy consumption. LAAM is statistically significantly better than BM25 and is indistinguishable from DeepSeek on average precision, though not on MAP (Friedman test, P<0.05 with post-hoc testing). Overall, our results demonstrate that selectively approximating LLM relevance judgments through active learning enables retrieval accuracy to be controlled directly through the evaluation (and consequently energy) budget. Rather than committing to either inexpensive (and less accurate) lexical retrieval or exhaustive (and expensive) LLM reranking, our framework exposes a continuous spectrum of operating points along the energy--accuracy curve, allowing practitioners to select how to trade retrieval quality with computational budget.

candidates.title: VisText-VLM2Plastic: A Bilingual Benchmark for Visual Grounding and Environmental Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support open-ended visual reasoning, yet their behavior in low-resource languages and sustainability-oriented domains remains underexplored. We introduce a controlled English–Bangla plastic-waste VQA benchmark comprising 402 image records derived from 136 base images and 2,412 question–answer pairs across five waste categories and three task types: recognition, visual description, and environmental reasoning. We evaluate GPT-4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B zero-shot using task-specific answer-quality metrics, bilingual consistency, and image ablation. Gemini 2.5 Flash yields the highest recognition point estimate, with 93.5% accuracy and 91.3% macro-F1. Across models, English normalized performance exceeds Bangla by 3.78 points on average, with the largest observed gap for environmental reasoning. Removing the image reduces normalized performance by 66.29 points for recognition, 52.89 for description, and 11.42 for environmental reasoning. The smaller environmental-reasoning ablation gap indicates that, in this benchmark, many environmental questions remain partly answerable from linguistic and domain priors. These results show why answer quality alone is insufficient for multilingual multimodal evaluation and motivate reporting cross-lingual consistency and sensitivity to visual evidence alongside conventional metrics.

candidates.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

candidates.title: AstroMemBench: A Benchmark for Memory Systems in Embodied Spacecraft Agents
candidates.abstract: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.

candidates.title: daVinci-Prover: Agent-Native Mid-Training for Formal Theorem Proving
candidates.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision, together with verifier-grounded agentic trajectories. We further introduce the daVinci-Prover harness, which enables models to construct proofs and interact with a Lean verifier in an isolated workspace, and use it to collect approximately 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Our mid-training recipe yields an average improvement of 13.7 points over the matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet. When applied to the Qwen3.5 series, our approach also yields strong performance across theorem-proving benchmarks and achieves near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction. The results highlight agent-native mid-training as an effective foundation for developing stronger interactive theorem-proving agents.

candidates.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
candidates.abstract: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.

candidates.title: Wanda-Guided Sparse Perturbations for Efficient Zeroth-Order Optimization
candidates.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models through forward-only evaluations, but high-dimensional random perturbations can limit optimization efficiency. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, making the selection of informative coordinates critical. We propose Wanda-Importance Sparsity-MeZO (WIS-MeZO), which uses Wanda weight--activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. We analyze support quality through gradient energy capture and relate it to gradient estimation and convergence. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Comparisons with random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations further highlight the importance of informative support selection.

candidates.title: Turning Multi-Agent Communication into Token-Level Credit with On Policy Self Distillation
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves problem solving in large language model multi-agent systems. Existing approaches overlook communication knowledge or compress it into scalar rewards, leaving coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise. OPSD4MAS converts future communication into fine-grained token-level credit through On Policy Self Distillation (OPSD). An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse-grained filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. The fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective. Our method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, while frozen-history injection diagnostics support fact utility. Together, these results support combining agent-level outcome guidance with communication-derived token-level credit. Code is available at https://github.com/Camel-Prince/OPSD4MAS.

candidates.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding
candidates.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier. It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware. Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ~10x energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14x below the uncached baseline). We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.

candidates.title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
candidates.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.

candidates.title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization
candidates.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.

candidates.title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

candidates.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
candidates.abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

candidates.title: SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection
candidates.abstract: The easy access to Large Language Models (LLMs) has made AI-generated texts on the web increasingly ubiquitous, making AI-text detection a crucial task. Prompts greatly influence the generation process, but existing detectors focus solely on the generated texts --- supervised methods learn from labeled texts only, and zero-shot methods rely on the text's probability distributions --- ignoring the underlying generation process, which limits their robustness in open-world scenarios. We introduce SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection, a novel framework for detecting AI-generated text that transfers better across datasets. Specifically, we measure the prompt's influence and use it as a discriminative signal. We characterize the prompt's influence by introducing a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) term that captures how much a prompt explains a text. Based on this quantity, SPADE trains one soft prompt per class to amplify the separation, and predicts the class whose prompt best explains the candidate text. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks against various detectors demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets.

candidates.title: SAGE-QA: Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Closed-Context Question Answering on SQuAD 2.0
candidates.abstract: Closed-context question answering (QA) requires a system to generate an answer strictly supported by a supplied passage, or to abstain when the passage lacks adequate evidence. SQuAD 2.0 is a widely used benchmark for this setting, scored by Exact Match (EM) i.e., character-level agreement with human reference spans after lexical normalization. For generative large language models (LLMs), however, an EM failure may reflect a valid paraphrase or an alternative passage-supported answer rather than a hallucination. The best prior leaderboard EM is approximately 91%, but evaluating generative models requires separating lexical divergence from factual error. We introduce SAGE-QA (Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Question Answering), a multi-tiered framework combining reference-based Semantic Equivalence Scoring (SES) and passage-based Re-Validation Scoring (RVS). On a fixed set of 10,000 SQuAD 2.0 validation examples, we compute EM and decision-matrix F1 from TP, TN, FP, and FN counts for zero-shot closed-weight frontier models and for open-weight models, untuned and fine-tuned. Zero-shot, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach 85.21 and 86.66 EM, outperforming untuned Llama 3 8B (56.88), gpt-oss-20b (66.28), and Llama 3.3 70B (71.39). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adds 21.19 to 34.06 EM points, raising these models to 90.94, 87.47, and 94.24 EM, respectively. Auditing the frontier models with SAGE-QA and an external LLM judge yields dataset-wide SES scores of 92.81 for Claude Opus 4.6 and 91.67 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and hybrid RVS scores, which combine benchmark credit with passage-based judge assessments, of 97.96 and 98.02. Fine-tuned open-weight models perform best, with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B surpassing the previous best known EM.

candidates.title: ROSETTA: Efficient and Accurate Privacy-Preserving LLM Decoding via Hybrid CKKS/TFHE Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Generative large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance on many real-world tasks such as code generation and question answering. These models predominantly rely on an autoregressive decoding strategy that generates output tokens sequentially. However, their pervasive deployment raises serious privacy concerns, motivating private inference frameworks based on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). A major limitation of existing FHE frameworks is their inefficiency in evaluating nonlinear operations, which incur substantial overhead and dominate the decode stage. In this paper, we propose ROSETTA, a hybrid CKKS/TFHE framework that overcomes this limitation. We first observe that nonlinear operations in the decode stage exhibit heterogeneous workload patterns, which can be handled effectively via a hybrid approach. We then realize this with two key contributions: 1) an adaptive segmented lookup-table protocol based on TFHE that enables efficient and accurate evaluation of nonlinear operations; and 2) a scheme-aware operator-selection framework that automatically assigns each nonlinear operator to CKKS or TFHE to minimize end-to-end decoding latency. We demonstrate that ROSETTA achieves up to $4.8\times$ Softmax speedup and $1.5$--$2.1\times$ end-to-end speedup over the SOTA framework CacheMir.

candidates.title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
candidates.abstract: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

candidates.title: POSTER: A Preliminary Study of LLM Distillation Inference
candidates.abstract: Unauthorized model distillation, in which a model is trained on the outputs of a proprietary large language model (LLM), is a growing threat to model providers. We study distillation inference: determining whether a suspect model was distilled from another model or trained independently. We formulate this problem as a hypothesis test and estimate the behavior expected under each hypothesis by training shadow models: distilled shadow models learn from the teacher's reasoning traces, whereas independent shadow models learn only from reference answers. The auditor measures how closely each model predicts the teacher's reasoning outputs and then uses the shadow models to convert the suspect's score into a calibrated p-value. In a preliminary study using Qwen2.5-7B as the teacher and Llama-3.2-3B for the suspects, our test achieves a true positive rate of 1.0 at a significance level of 0.02. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using distillation inference to detect distillation attacks.
