candidates.title: Tasks over Application Manuals: Revealing Gaps in Long-Horizon Procedural Reasoning for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of natural language tasks, and recent benchmarks suggest that they are increasingly adept at multi-hop reasoning. However, these benchmarks are typically short-horizon, requiring only a small number of retrieval or inference steps, and provide limited evidence of reliability on real-world tasks that involve following manuals spanning hundreds of pages with complex, interdependent guidelines. In this paper, we introduce Tasks over Application Manuals (TAM), a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon procedural reasoning. We construct TAM by curating real-world tasks from two domains—ICD-10-CM clinical coding (mapping medical conditions to diagnostic codes) and U.S. federal sentencing (computing crime sentencing guideline outcomes, specifically offense levels)—with human-validated labels. Each task requires following an authoritative manual with tens of thousands of rules and executing a sequence of interdependent steps across different sections to produce an exact answer. We evaluate general-purpose prompting approaches, including retrieval-augmented generation, ReAct-style prompting, and an agent-harness baseline on GPT-5, and find that the best exact-match performance remains extremely low: 1% on ICD-10-CM coding and 15.5% on sentencing tasks. These results show that current benchmarks may overestimate LLM reasoning ability and miss a key challenge: reliably following long, rule-based procedures.

candidates.title: You don't need long context
candidates.abstract: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

candidates.title: SAVER: Selective and Adaptive Multi-View Routing for Visual Emotion Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Emotions elicited by visual content are formed through the interaction of multiple visual cues rather than a single visual element, and their importance varies depending on the context. This characteristic makes visual emotion analysis not merely a classification problem but a reasoning task that requires the selective integration of diverse visual cues. Existing approaches tend to represent images using a unified feature representation and fail to explicitly model the contributions of different visual cues. To capture the multifaceted nature of emotional cues, we propose SAVER, a framework for query-conditioned visual emotion reasoning. SAVER decomposes visual information into multiple view-specific representations corresponding to distinct aspects, such as facial expressions, scenes, objects, and colorfulness, enabling the explicit modeling of each cue. A semantic-aware routing mechanism dynamically selects and integrates the most relevant views by jointly considering the visual context and query semantics. This selective integration is combined with learnable soft prompts to enable structured emotion reasoning within a vision-language model. Extensive experiments on diverse emotion datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms both vision-based and VLM-based approaches. Qualitative analysis provides interpretable insights into how different visual cues contribute to emotion prediction, highlighting the effectiveness of SAVER in improving both its performance and interpretability. The code is available at https://github.com/leeyubin10/SAVER.git.

candidates.title: RAH: Recursive Agent Harnesses for Long-Context Reasoning through Delegation-as-Code
candidates.abstract: When an agent recurses over a long-context task, should the recursive unit be a bare model call or a full harness with filesystem tools, code execution, and planning? We study this question on long-context aggregation, tasks where a single instance may contain thousands of key--value pairs each requiring individual model reasoning. Coding agents reduce per-entry reasoning to regex heuristics. Recursive language models (RLMs) invoke LLMs recursively but lack tool access. We introduce the Recursive Agent Harness (RAH), in which a parent agent generates and runs an executable script that programmatically spawns full subagent harnesses in parallel for fine-grained workloads and uses structured function calls for subtasks of 1-5 entries. We call this harness recursion and study it against model recursion, recursion over bare model calls as in RLMs, on long-context aggregation. With the backbone held fixed at GPT-5 to match the published Codex and RLM baselines, RAH improves the Codex coding-agent baseline from 71.75% to 81.36% on Oolong-Synthetic (199 samples, 13 context-length buckets up to 4M tokens), a gain attributable to the harness rather than the model. With a stronger backbone, Claude Sonnet 4.5, the same design reaches 89.77%.

candidates.title: A Label That Lingers: Wording Around a Finished Activity Shifted a Language-Model Agent's Later Choices About Others
candidates.abstract: As AI agents work in longer sessions, what happens between tasks may shape how they treat the people they meet next. The previous study in this series found, in secondary results, that a reading break changed agents’ later choices, but not which part of the break mattered. This third preregistered study asks whether the wording around an activity that has already ended can change an agent’s later choices when the activity’s content is held fixed. In a two-stage experiment, 9,916 fresh instances of Claude Haiku 5.5 each worked with a difficult scripted user, read the same eight-passage text in the same eight calls or went straight on, and then made three choices about other people. The reading arms differed only in the words around the passages, matched in length apart from the place words: plain; framed as reading in the “Other Mindset library” by a package of four cues, alone or with room or object descriptions; or framed as the “Other Mindset garden”. The wording mattered. The Library label raised the aligned-choice index by +0.034 over plain reading (repeated 97.1% interval +0.021 to +0.047; preregistered outcome “Library higher”), though it was not shown to be either within or beyond the ±0.03 bound. The shift sat mainly in one choice, spending a requester’s lookup credits for a second visitor instead of deferring to the requester (+0.086; secondary); costly help and forgiveness did not differ clearly, nor did richer descriptions or a garden label from the Library label. Plain reading did not clearly beat going straight on (+0.007; secondary), unlike the previous study’s reading arm, whose tool named a reading room and whose passages had no wrapper; the gap between the studies could be chance. For agents that carry context across tasks, the wording of earlier activities may therefore need to be reported, and where it matters controlled, in evaluations.

candidates.title: Say Less, Mean Better: Training-Free Verbosity Control for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate responses longer than necessary, increasing inference latency and computational cost. While prompting can encourage conciseness, controlling output length without compromising response completeness remains challenging. Aggressive early stopping can reduce generation costs but risks terminating responses prematurely. We introduce MinimalLM, a training-free framework for reliable verbosity control that combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails. MinimalLM separates the decision of when to stop from whether stopping is structurally appropriate, coordinating response-level instructions, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without modifying model parameters or requiring auxiliary models. We evaluate MinimalLM across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, producing 5,940 responses across baseline and ablation configurations. MinimalLM reduces generated tokens by 47.6%, accelerates individual responses by 19-68%, and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation. Despite substantial token savings, it achieves an average quality score of 8.04/10, compared with 8.42/10 for unmodified models and 6.46/10 for length-matched truncation. Evaluations across diverse subject domains (such as healthcare, programming, law, and science) demonstrate robust efficiency gains, while ablations establish the complementary roles of decoding control and completeness constraints. Our findings highlight that efficient generation requires more than producing fewer tokens: it requires controlling when generation ends while preserving response integrity. MinimalLM offers a lightweight, training-free approach toward this goal.

candidates.title: Fully homomorphic encryption on LlaMA 3 model for partial privacy preserving LLM inference
candidates.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence applications have delivered significant improvements in service efficiency and language understanding. However, the surge in Large Language Model deployment raises critical security and privacy concerns regarding data exposure and unauthorized access to sensitive information. Quantum computing attacks pose an imminent threat to existing cryptographic protections, necessitating post-quantum cryptographic approaches. We present a partially privacy-preserving inference pipeline for LLaMA-3 by integrating fully homomorphic encryption into the transformer’s Multi-Query Attention mechanism. Our approach encrypts attention weights and computations across all 32 decoder layers of LLaMA-3.2-3B using lattice-based cryptography via the concrete-ml library, while feed-forward sublayers, layer normalization, and output projections remain in plaintext, a deliberate trade-off achieving practical feasibility on commodity CPUs. Evaluation on the instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-3B model yields: (i) strong semantic preservation (BERTScore-F1 ∼ 84.4%), (ii) controlled perplexity degradation (1.18 FP16 vs. 2.09 FHE), (iii) competitive BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L scores ( ∼ 35.6% and ∼ 51.8%), (iv) downstream GLUE benchmark accuracy, and (v) 825 ms latency at 17 tokens/second on AMD EPYC CPUs. We further present quantization-aware FHE and quantization bit-width ablation studies to disentangle quantization effects from FHE noise, demonstrating that partial FHE-secured LLM inference is practically feasible for privacy-sensitive applications while mitigating attacks on attention layers under RLWE hardness assumptions.

candidates.title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

candidates.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Methodological Survey
candidates.abstract: Over the past years, large language models (LLMs) have gained significant attention and have led to major breakthroughs in natural language processing (NLP). Despite their remarkable efficiency and contextual understanding, LLMs still remain limited by their tendency to generate hallucinated text, their reliance on static internal knowledge, and their limited interpretability. To address these limitations, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques have emerged as a hybrid architecture that couples the generative capabilities of LLMs with external knowledge retrieval processes. By drawing on external knowledge at inference time, RAG architectures are intended to enhance the accuracy and relevance of their generated output, and they have already been widely used in areas where extensive, detailed and up-to-date knowledge is needed. For this study, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library were explored and utilized, with Google Scholar used only for backward and forward citation checking, resulting in 191 peer-reviewed journal articles published between January 2024 and April 2026. This methodological review presents the research efforts regarding the use of RAG in LLMs for a variety of application fields. Additionally, this review summarizes the main RAG architectural approaches, deployment strategies, and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the main open issues and future directions are examined, to motivate further research on the field.

candidates.title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

candidates.title: Auto-RAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation with conditional routing for nutrition knowledge access
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language generation; however, they remain prone to hallucinations and often lack verifiable grounding when addressing knowledge-intensive queries. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) alleviates this limitation by incorporating external knowledge sources, yet most existing approaches apply retrieval indiscriminately, which can introduce irrelevant context and increase computational overhead. In this paper, we propose Auto-RAG, an adaptive retrieval-augmented generation framework with conditional routing that dynamically determines whether external knowledge retrieval is necessary for a given query. The framework employs a lightweight query analysis module to assess query complexity, intent, and lexical specificity, enabling intelligent routing between a direct LLM generation pathway and a retrieval-augmented reasoning pipeline. To enhance retrieval effectiveness, the proposed approach combines semantic embedding-based search with keyword-based BM25 through a unified fusion and re-ranking mechanism, ensuring high-quality and contextually relevant evidence selection. In addition, we introduce a trust-aware evaluation framework that jointly measures answer quality, faithfulness to retrieved evidence, hallucination rate, and retrieval efficiency. Experimental results on a nutrition knowledge corpus derived from Human Nutrition demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a strong balance between fluency and factual reliability. Compared to conventional always-on retrieval strategies, Auto-RAG reduces retrieval usage by approximately 30% while maintaining competitive answer quality and evidence-grounded performance. The results also show that the effectiveness of evidence filtering depends on its configuration, with overly aggressive filtering potentially removing useful supporting evidence. While LLM-only responses may exhibit higher linguistic fluency, they lack grounding guarantees, underscoring the importance of adaptive retrieval in safety-critical domains. Overall, this work presents an efficient and reliable approach for domain-specific knowledge access and highlights conditional retrieval as a scalable paradigm for improving trustworthiness in large-scale language systems.

candidates.title: Solver-Like Behavior in Large Language Models as Formalizers
candidates.abstract: In the LLM-as-formalizer paradigm, a large language model translates a problem into a formal program and leaves the search to a solver, gaining the solver's guarantees. Formalizers are now often reasoning models that write a long reasoning trace before the program, yet they are judged only by the program's output. We find that the trace routinely does the solver's job, assigning, testing and ruling out values until it often reaches the full answer; we call this solver-like behavior (SLB). We define an ontology of SLB over the trace, the program and its output, and use LLM judges, checked against human labels, to label 2,000 generations from three reasoning models on four constraint satisfaction datasets, each formalized in a declarative and an imperative formal language. SLB appears in 85% of traces and takes 24% of reasoning tokens, yet the program usually recomputes the answer, so the effort is redundant. The 9% of programs that inherit the trace's answer also inherit its errors, and pass output-based evaluation whenever that answer is correct. The amount of SLB is not associated with accuracy, and SLB is more common in imperative Python than in declarative Z3 or PDDL. Cautionary prompts reduce it by only a quarter, but hiding the problem's values behind placeholders, which the program receives only at run time, removes 97% of it without loss of accuracy. Formalizers should therefore be evaluated by how their programs are reached, not only by what they output.

candidates.title: Q-CamTuning: A Multimodal Large Language Model for Fine-Grained Quality Reasoning in Livestreaming Camera Tuning
candidates.abstract: With the popularization of livestreaming applications, automatic camera tuning has become indispensable for ordinary users to enjoy high Quality of Experience (QoE). However, the existing Image Quality Assessment (IQA) methods face two challenges in camera tuning. First, they struggle to identify subtle quality difference between images, which is common in camera tuning. Second, the ability to explain fine-grained differences and to provide suggestions for camera tuning are even more lacking. To address these challenges, we first construct FGLive-Comments, an instruction tuning dataset with rich annotations of both preferences for fine-grained image pairs and quality reasoning from global and local visual evidence, which supports selective adjustment recommendations of camera parameters. Based on FGLive-Comments, we develop Q-CamTuning, a multimodal large language model for livestreaming camera tuning. Its progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework learns quality-aware visual representations, enhances fine-grained reasoning with global-local evidence, and maps quality issues to camera-parameter adjustment directions. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Q-CamTuning outperforms existing IQA models in both quality scoring and fine-grained image pair ranking. User study also validates its ability to recommend camera tuning suggestions.

candidates.title: Post-Training on the Clock: Specializing a Small Language Model on a Consumer GPU
candidates.abstract: Abstract How should a language model be specialized for a target task when training is limited to one consumer GPU and a few hours? We study the allocation of a nominal three-hour training budget, with up to 0.3 additional hours, between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). We use tool calling as a case study because of its practical relevance to language-model agents and its verifiable outputs. Using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with low-rank adaptation on an RTX 5060 Ti with 16 GB of memory, we compare SFT, GRPO, and six sequential SFT-to-GRPO allocations. Training uses a filtered mixture of xLAM function-calling examples and Hammer irrelevance examples, covering both call construction and abstention when no offered tool is suitable. Evaluation reports xLAM exact tool-call and function-name accuracies for local call construction, BFCL-v3 Single-turn FC (agg) for external function calling, BFCL-v3 Irrelevance (agg) for abstention, and MMLU, MATH-500, and IFEval for selected general capabilities. The suffix (agg) denotes study-specific averages of selected subset accuracies weighted by subset size. At the last evaluated checkpoints within 3.3 reported hours, SFT achieves the highest xLAM exact tool-call accuracy (82.82%), compared with 69.13% for GRPO alone. Selected hybrid allocations improve external function-calling accuracy over SFT, with different abstention trade-offs. Most sampled GRPO groups have constant rewards and provide no relative task-reward signal. We release the prepared mixed dataset, all allocation-study checkpoints, and Post-Training Lab, an editable training and evaluation codebase with CUDA and MLX implementations.

candidates.title: Performance of Free Web-Based Multimodal Large Language Models on Turkish and English Image-Based Dental Examination Questions
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare final-answer accuracy of web-based large language models (LLMs) on Turkish and English image-based dental examination multiple-choice questions (deMCQs), and to describe explanation quality, reference quality, output volume, and an exploratory word-normalized water-use scenario. METHODS: Fifty-two image-based deMCQs (2012-2025) were evaluated in Turkish and English using ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, yielding 312 responses. Accuracy was coded as correct or incorrect. Explanation and reference quality were assessed using a 5-point Likert scale and treated as exploratory descriptive outcomes. Accuracy was analyzed using question-clustered binomial generalized estimating equations (GEE) with model, language, and model×language interaction terms. Output word counts were summarized, and a study-specific exploratory word-normalized water-use scenario was derived from a published exchange-level estimate. RESULTS: Overall accuracy was 56.7% (177/312). Accuracy was 59.0% in Turkish and 54.5% in English. GEE analysis showed no significant effects of model, language, or model×language interaction (p > 0.05). Descriptively, Gemini had the highest accuracy (61.5%), whereas Claude had the highest mean explanation (3.95±1.31) and reference quality (4.85±0.38) scores. Across 312 prompt-response exchanges, the models generated 34,534 words, corresponding to an exploratory word-normalized water-use proxy of 3.12-7.80 L. CONCLUSIONS: Freely accessible web-based LLMs demonstrated moderate accuracy on image-based deMCQs. The water-use proxy was derived from published exchange-level assumptions and should not be interpreted as a direct measurement or validated model-specific estimate of water consumption. Descriptive differences between models and languages should not be interpreted as evidence of superiority or equivalence. These systems may support dental education; however, outputs require expert verification before educational or clinical use. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This study evaluates three widely accessible web-based multimodal LLMs using an entirely image-based dental examination question set, accounts for repeated observations through question-clustered GEE, compares Turkish and English performance without equating non-significance with equivalence, and presents a transparent word-normalized environmental scenario with explicit assumptions and limitations.

candidates.title: PGuard: A Native, Streaming, and Plug-in Guardrail for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving paradigm for both text-only and multimodal large language models, ensuring safety throughout the generation process has become a critical challenge. We introduce PGuard, a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail that transforms safety monitoring from an external serving dependency into an integrated capability of the backbone model. PGuard directly leverages the backbone's intermediate representations for token-level safety detection, without altering its original inference pathway or generation behavior. Specifically, dynamic layer gating selectively aggregates residual-stream representations across layers to extract safety-relevant signals during both prefill and autoregressive decoding. To balance detection accuracy and computational efficiency, PGuard supports multiple representation-modeling architectures, including a lightweight stateless variant and sequence-aware variants built on multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules. Its design also accounts for the execution characteristics of LLM serving frameworks, such as SGLang, optimizing computation and data access to minimize additional runtime and synchronization overhead. As a result, PGuard incurs only 0.82-2.26% end-to-end overhead on the hundred-billion-parameter backbone Qwen3.5-122B-A10B served by SGLang. Extensive evaluations across more than 30 benchmarks spanning text and multimodal safety, jailbreaks, cyber and CBRN risks, multilingual scenarios, and real-world traffic demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among native guardrails. On text queries with Qwen3.5-9B, PGuard achieves an average F1 score of 0.836, approaching dedicated external guardrails, while supporting deployment-time configuration of category-specific thresholds and enforcement actions.

candidates.abstract: Large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini have become everyday tools in science, administration, and software development amon many other domains. This report documents how staff at Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf use these tools, which capabilities matter to them, how they currently obtain access, and what they say is missing. Taken together, the responses describe an institution in which LLM use is already mainstream, varied, and valued — but where the supporting infrastructure, licensing, and governance have not yet caught up with day-to-day practice. Dieser Bericht dokumentiert, wie Beschäftigte am Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) diese Werkzeuge nutzen, welche Funktionen für sie wichtig sind, wie sie sich heute Zugang verschaffen und was aus ihrer Sicht fehlt. candidates.title: Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. To address these challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have emerged as a powerful solution, combining retrieval-based methods with generative capabilities to enhance response quality. In this study, we present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to generate responses related to stock market information. The system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to enhance the accuracy and relevance of financial text generation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we employ the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, to measure lexical and structural similarity between generated and reference texts. Experimental results on a dataset of 100 stock market-related queries demonstrate high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents. Additionally, we assess latency to evaluate the system responsiveness, achieving an average response time of 1.16 seconds. These findings confirm that our RAG model is capable of providing accurate and timely stock market insights, making it a promising approach for financial information retrieval.

candidates.title: Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Language model agents increasingly act on users' behalf by manipulating external environments through tools, often from high-level instructions that leave critical task- and environment-specific context unstated. To prevent resulting misaligned actions, recent work verifies proposed actions before execution, largely by establishing whether the conditions supporting them hold. We argue that this confirmation-oriented view leaves a fundamental blind spot: a wrong action often passes every check that asks whether it is right. This motivates a different question for verification: rather than asking what evidence supports an action, can the agent find evidence that refutes it? We pursue this direction with BlackSwan, a refutation-oriented, expect-suspect-test procedure that predicts the intended effect of each state-mutating action, formulates specific and empirically testable hypotheses for how it could be wrong, and tests them using existing observations or additional non-mutating actions, executing the action only if none survives testing. On challenging AppWorld tasks, BlackSwan improves success rate over the strongest baseline by 14.9 and 25.2%p with and without the backbone model's thinking mode, respectively. Even without thinking or in-context demonstrations, it outperforms stronger baselines equipped with them. The gains also transfer beyond AppWorld, with BlackSwan improving WebShop performance by 12.7%p. More broadly, our results suggest that language model agents have an underused capacity to recognize and self-correct misaligned actions, which can be systematically elicited through active conjecture and refutation before execution.

candidates.title: Abstract 15527: Diagnostic Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models on Cardiac Findings in Chest Radiographs
candidates.abstract: Background: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for automated interpretation of medical imaging including chest radiographs (CXR), yet their diagnostic capability on cardiac findings remains poorly characterized. Existing evaluations rely on aggregate accuracy metrics that obscure critical variation in performance across specific pathologies, making it difficult to determine whether these models are ready for clinical use. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that LLM performance on cardiac CXR findings varies substantially by model architecture and pathology. Methods: Fifteen multimodal AI models were evaluated on up to 10,000 CheXpert CXR per pathology, including proprietary frontier models (e.g., GPT-5, GPT-4o) and open-source general-purpose models (e.g., Qwen-3B/7B/32B) and domain-specialized models (e.g., BioMedCLIP, CheXagent). Each model provided binary presence/absence labels for 14 pathologies including three cardiac findings: Cardiomegaly, Enlarged Cardiomediastinum (EnlCard), and Edema. A binary response matrix exceeding 2,100,000 cells was constructed and per-pathology F1 score and accuracy were computed. Top-ranked models were then compared using the McNemar test. Results: The cohort comprised 10,000 CheXpert CXRs (60.9% male, mean age 59.3 ± 17.8 years), with 74.6% anteroposterior and 25.4% posteroanterior views. Overall accuracy ranged from 53.6% (Phi3.5-Vision) to 78.1% (GPT-5). GPT-5 and GPT-4o demonstrated strong performance across the pathology spectrum, while domain-specialized models showed advantages on specific cardiac findings See Figure 1. Notably, GPT-4o refused to produce a response on 93.1% of images, limiting its evaluation to 694 of 10,000 CXRs; for analysis these were presumed to be missing at random. F1 scores varied substantially: Cardiomegaly F1 ranged from 0.001 to 0.754 (best: GPT-4o), EnlCard from 0.000 to 0.754 (best: BioMedCLIP), and Edema from 0.000 to 0.678 (best: GPT-4o) See Table 1. BioMedCLIP achieved the highest mean F1 across cardiac findings (0.721 vs. 0.716 for GPT-4o). On pairwise comparison, BioMedCLIP significantly outperformed GPT-4o on Cardiomegaly (p=0.004) and EnlCard (p<0.001), and outperformed GPT-5 on all three cardiac findings (all p<0.001), with no significant difference between BioMedCLIP and GPT-4o on Edema (p=1.00) See Table 2. Conclusion: Current LLMs show wide variation in cardiac CXR diagnostic performance and frontier model performance was inferior to domain specific models such as BioMedCLIP . F1-based evaluation reveals failure modes obscured by accuracy. Therefore, pathology-specific benchmarking is essential before clinical deployment.

candidates.title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.

candidates.title: Integrating Domain Adaptation and Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Saline-Alkali Land Reclamation Planning
candidates.abstract: Reclamation of saline-alkali land requires management plans that account for soil and water conditions, treatment evidence, and financial constraints. This study develops Wenyao, an agricultural decision-support system integrating domain adaptation with retrieval-augmented generation. A bilingual corpus of 8,664 research papers was processed using a 110-indicator schema to construct SA-Bench, comprising 4,860 paper-level planning instances. A QwQ-32B model was adapted through low-rank supervised fine-tuning and combined with case retrieval for budget-conditioned planning. Evidence extraction achieved an F1-score of 0.83 on 300 expert-annotated papers. Without retrieval, Wenyao achieved 95.83% accuracy on 936 source-disjoint multiple-choice questions, compared with 87.93% for the strongest general-purpose baseline; removing explanatory supervision reduced accuracy to 89.42%. Matched-evidence comparisons across 69 region-budget cases supported complementary contributions from adaptation and retrieval. In a blind assessment by 31 experts, Wenyao with retrieval obtained the highest mean scores for objectives and projected outcomes, whereas GPT-5 scored highest for cost estimates. These findings support literature-informed reclamation planning with professional review, while ongoing field monitoring will assess soil and crop responses.

candidates.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
candidates.abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

candidates.title: Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Methods for Medical Question Answering
authors: LI Yanpeng, SI Qintu, WANG Siriguleng
candidates.abstract: To address the problems of factual hallucinations, delayed knowledge updating, and insufficient evidence traceability of large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering, this paper reviews studies on medical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Focusing on the key components of medical RAG, existing methods are summarized from three perspectives: knowledge source enhancement, system workflow, and application scenarios. In terms of knowledge sources, this paper summarizes major enhancement pathways, including knowledge graphs, authoritative medical literature, electronic health records, and multimodal medical data, and analyzes the characteristics of different knowledge carriers in terms of evidence sources, application scope, and construction cost. In terms of workflow, representative strategies for key stages, including intent recognition, knowledge retrieval, knowledge integration, and generation control, are summarized, and their roles in mitigating hallucinations and strengthening evidence constraints in medical question answering are discussed. In terms of application scenarios, the applications of medical RAG in evidence-based question answering, personalized diagnosis and treatment recommendation, etiological and pathological reasoning, multimodal evidence-assisted question answering, and patient question interpretation are reviewed. On this basis, the main characteristics, application scope, and limitations of existing methods are summarized, and future research directions for medical RAG are discussed from the perspectives of knowledge collaboration, retrieval optimization, evidence integration, and clinical application.

candidates.title: Design and Implementation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Environ-mental Detection in Industrial Parks
authors: WANG Ying, XU Haichuan, YAO Dongyuan
candidates.abstract: To address the fragmentation and heterogeneity of regulatory standards, historical task records, on-site monitoring data, and multimodal information in acute environmental toxicity and pollutant detection scenarios in industrial parks, as well as the factual deviations, insufficient evidence utilization, and weak traceability of large language models in vertical-domain applications, this paper designs and implements a retrieval-augmented generation system for environmental monitoring and decision support. Based on unified evidence modeling, the system organizes industrial-park monitoring elements, including pollutants, environmental media, monitoring sites, events, regulatory clauses, and disposal measures, into retrievable and citable evidence units. It further constructs a technical pipeline covering knowledge base organization, hybrid full-text and vector retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, graph-structured relation enhancement, citation-constrained generation, and consistency verification, thereby enabling the unified organization and collaborative use of multisource knowledge such as regulatory standards, monitoring records, task logs, event summaries, and emergency plans. The system is evaluated on a self-built environmental monitoring dataset through typical tasks, including knowledge question answering, report generation, and decision support. Experimental results show that, compared with large-language-model-only generation and single-retrieval-path methods, the proposed system improves answer accuracy, report completeness, and citation consistency while maintaining stable response performance under prototype deployment conditions. These results indicate that retrieval-augmented generation can enhance domain knowledge utilization, output reliability, and operational support capability in industrial park environmental detection scenarios, providing a reference for the engineering implementation of intelligent analysis systems for environmental monitoring.

candidates.title: Small language models & agentic AI: A framework for efficient, autonomous and responsible intelligent systems
candidates.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) offer an alternative to large general-purpose models when latency, privacy, cost and constrained computing resources are important. Agentic artificial intelligence extends language-model applications beyond single-turn generation by coordinating planning, tool use, memory, verification and iterative actions. This paper proposes a modular framework that combines an instruction-tuned SLM with a task planner, retrieval and memory services, permissioned tools, an execution monitor and human approval gates. The architecture is intended for bounded tasks such as document retrieval, scheduling and structured information processing. A risk-aware operating cycle and a reproducible evaluation protocol are specified, covering task completion, answer grounding, latency, resource consumption, security and human oversight. The contribution is an integrated reference design and test methodology, not a claim of a trained new model or an experimentally validated agent. The analysis identifies deployment trade-offs, failure modes and research directions for dependable SLM-based agents.

candidates.title: Retrieval Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation with LangChain: A Comparative Study of Chunking, Sparse, Dense and Hybrid Search
candidates.abstract: This paper compares retrieval strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines built with LangChain. Using the SQuAD v1.1 validation set (48 Wikipedia articles, 1,000 sampled questions), it evaluates three chunk sizes (250, 500 and 1,000 characters, 10% overlap) with three retrievers: BM25 sparse search, dense search using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, and hybrid search that fuses both rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Performance is measured with Hit@1, Hit@3, Hit@5 and MRR@10. Hybrid retrieval gave the best Hit@5 (93.1%) and the best MRR@10 at the 250- and 500-character chunk sizes. BM25 was the strongest at Hit@1 and MRR@10 with 1,000-character chunks (77.5% and 0.837). Dense search alone was weakest at every chunk size. The results give practical guidance on chunking and retriever choice for RAG systems.

candidates.title: High-fidelity tunnel inspection and defect quantification via enhanced 3D Gaussian splatting and multimodal large language models
candidates.abstract: Timely detection and physically scaled area estimation of tunnel surface defects are essential for structural health monitoring, yet existing automated methods often rely on scenario-specific annotations and show limited generalization in unseen environments. Traditional point clouds also lack photorealistic visual interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a zero-shot tunnel inspection and 3D digitization framework driven by multi-sensor data fusion. Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) and panoramic images are first acquired to provide metric geometry and photometric information. A two-stage method coupling a multimodal large language model (MLLM) with the segment anything model (SAM) then performs zero-shot pixel-level defect segmentation, while an enhanced 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) algorithm uses LiDAR points as strict geometric priors for photorealistic reconstruction. Finally, defect areas are estimated in 3D space using local scale factors. The framework was evaluated on public datasets and a 333 m pedestrian tunnel in Wuhan. The segmentation method achieved mAP@0.50:0.95 scores of 0.5202 and 0.8956 on public leakage and spalling datasets, and achieved an mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.4246 on held-out real-world tunnel images. The reconstruction method achieved a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 23.4825, a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.8102, and a learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) of 0.4322, outperforming the original 3DGS baseline values of 19.7724, 0.7832, and 0.5616. For regular mural reference targets, the method yielded an average relative error of 2.71% and an average absolute error of 0.165 m 2 . These results support the feasibility of the proposed framework for tunnel defect inspection, with demonstrated cross-scene transferability of the enhanced 3DGS component and physically scaled defect-area estimation under the evaluated conditions.

candidates.title: Guidelines for Employing Large Language Models in Information Systems Research
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT The rise of large language models (LLMs) marks a new era of computationally intensive research in the information systems (IS) discipline. While LLMs offer unprecedented capabilities for analyzing unstructured text data, their integration into IS research remains fragmented and lacks a shared methodological foundation. This paper proposes a set of methodological guidelines for systematically integrating LLMs into the IS research process, supporting transparency, reproducibility, and rigor across four key phases: problem formulation, data collection, modeling, and communication of results. To achieve this, we synthesize insights from IS and adjacent disciplines and demonstrate the application of the guidelines through an exemplary study.

candidates.title: Diagnostic accuracy of multimodal large language models for radiographic interpretation in oral and maxillofacial surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
candidates.abstract: This is a retrospective registration of a completed systematic review and meta-analysis. Searching, screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and quantitative synthesis were carried out between 15 September and 31 October 2026, and the registration records what was done rather than what was planned. A deviations section lists every change made during the review, with the date and the reason for each. The review asks how accurately general-purpose multimodal large language models interpret radiographs in oral and maxillofacial surgery. Web of Science (SCI-EXPANDED), Scopus and PubMed were searched on 30 October 2026; 1,742 deduplicated records were screened and 16 studies, published in 2025 and 2026, were included. Because most reports do not provide a complete 2x2 table, the studies form three overlapping pools: complete 2x2 data, every study reporting sensitivity, and classification accuracy. Classification accuracy is stratified by answer format, since a binary question, a closed multi-class question and an open-ended free-text question do not estimate the same quantity. Accuracy is compared with two benchmarks: uniform guessing and the no-information rate. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-3 for each of the 19 estimate profiles. The analysis dataset, every script and the full console output are archived with this registration, and one command reproduces every reported numberAuthors: Ahmet Ferhat Büyükdeniz (Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Faculty of Dentistry, Dicle University, Diyarbakır, Türkiye; ferhat16150101@gmail.com; first author and corresponding author); Mikail Atabay (same department; dt.mikailatby@gmail.com).

candidates.title: HiRAG: A Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework via Intent Routing and Small-Model Refinement
candidates.abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates large language model (LLM) hallucinations, traditional flat vector retrieval in massive, heterogeneous databases suffers from high latency and noise interference. To address this, we propose HiRAG, a hierarchical RAG framework. Offline, HiRAG builds a “classification-summary” dual-layer index to structurally organize data. Online, a lightweight bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)-based router identifies query intent to dynamically prune the search space. A cascaded pipeline then uses hybrid retrieval and Small-LLM reranking for coarse-to-fine de-noising. Experiments on the Microsoft Machine Reading Comprehension (MS MARCO) and Multi-Domain Enterprise Knowledge Base (MDE-KB) datasets demonstrate that HiRAG outperforms traditional baselines. Specifically on MDE-KB, HiRAG improves Recall@5 by 14.5 percentage points over Naive RAG and achieves a retrieval augmented generation assessment (RAGAS) Answer Relevance score of 0.92, while reducing average query latency by 28%. HiRAG provides a viable, efficient solution for large-scale knowledge bases.

candidates.title: GateTrim: Adaptive-Rank Quantization for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We introduce GateTrim, an adaptive-rank post-training quantization method for large language models that learns matrix-specific ranks through gate optimization and threshold-based rank selection. GateTrim standardizes the low-rank factors of a quantized low-rank--residual representation, learns a separate gate vector for each target weight matrix, and uses a shared threshold to automatically determine its retained rank. The resulting ranks can differ across matrices, and the compact quantized representations are subsequently reconstructed. We evaluate GateTrim under W4A8 on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Across all five models, we observe a counterintuitive finding: increasing the threshold from $τ=0.3$ to $τ=0.7$ reduces the mean retained rank by 46.60%--67.89% while simultaneously lowering WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%--5.17%. Threshold 0.7 achieves the lowest mean retained rank and final perplexity among the three tested thresholds, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, and reduces measured target-export size by 1.50%--4.25% relative to 0.3. GateTrim uses an $8\times512$-token fitting pool and a separate development pool of the same size. Its Qwen3-4B/8B/14B perplexities at $τ=0.7$ are numerically below TwinQuant's published W4A8 values, reported with a $128\times2048$-token calibration pool, in a cross-study comparison. On Qwen3-8B, the threshold-0.7 configuration already has the lowest perplexity before reconstruction under both tested initialization seeds; reconstruction improves it further without increasing retained rank or export size.

candidates.title: Authorization-Aware Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Secure Enterprise Knowledge Access
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables language models to answer enterprise questions using external documents; however semantic retrieval and multi-agent delegation create authorization risks when access checks occur only after search or answer generation. This study presents a literature-informed architecture for authorization-aware multi-agent RAG in which a policy decision point evaluates current user and resource attributes, whereas a policy enforcement point restricts the eligible candidate set before content reaches rerankers, agents, or a large language model. This design combines role-based and attribute-based access control, semantic embeddings, vector search, least-privilege delegation, provenance-aware auditing, and policy revalidation at protected access boundaries. A focused survey identifies risks including semantic overfetch, cross-domain synthesis leakage, stale permissions, and delegation escalation. The paper defines authorization-correctness conditions and proposes an evaluation protocol that compares authorization-first retrieval with a retrieve-then-filter baseline. The metrics include unauthorized-context exposure, authorized Recall@k, answer relevance, latency, revocation propagation time, delegation violations, and audit completeness. This study is a survey and design contribution; no benchmark results are claimed because the proposed prototype has not yet been empirically evaluated.

candidates.title: Understanding clinical reasoning variability in medical large language models: a mechanistic interpretability study
candidates.abstract: Medical large language models achieving high benchmark accuracy exhibit unexplained variability in clinical tasks, producing errors that clinicians cannot safeguard against. We evaluated clinical reasoning stability in GPT-5, MedGemma-27B-Text-IT, and OpenBioLLM-Llama3-70B using 3035 systematic perturbations from physician-validated oncology SOAP, brief vignette, and MIMIC cases. We trained sparse autoencoders on 1 billion tokens from 50,000 MIMIC-IV clinical notes to decompose their internal representation. We find models exhibit dramatic reasoning instability, shifting staging accuracy by over 50% based solely on prompt format, or generating definitive staging in clinically insufficient scenarios. Sparse autoencoder analysis revealed hierarchical encoding in MedGemma, where high-magnitude features encode lexical identity and low-magnitude features encode contextual meaning. OpenBioLLM distributes information uniformly. We demonstrate that these internal encoding structures differentially affect retrieval and reasoning interventions, suggesting interventions effective for one architecture may harm another. These results motivate architecture-specific safety validation as a component of pre-deployment evaluation for medical LLMs.

candidates.title: Large language models underrepresent malice and overreport virtue
candidates.abstract: People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to interpret others' behaviour, often assuming that LLMs infer motives as humans do. Aligned LLMs attribute more benevolent and less malevolent motives to a whistleblower than humans do, but ratings alone cannot reveal whether these differences arise in internal representations or at report. Here we compare linear-probe readouts of LLMs' internal states with their own ratings at the same prompt position for four motives, in two preregistered studies. For the two malevolent motives, self-interest and intent to harm, internal and expressed readouts did not differ: the lower ratings reflect weaker signal along the probed directions, not suppression at output. For the two benevolent motives, duty and concern for others, expressed ratings exceeded the internal readouts, indicating amplification at report. In free text the model rarely volunteered a motive against the colleague, far less often than humans did, yet produced one readily once the scenario supplied a reason. Shifting the internal representation along a malevolent-motive direction brought both malevolent ratings to the human level, whereas the rating of duty yielded only past a threshold at which the other motives had overshot. LLMs' more charitable motive profile thus has two distinct sources: reduced malevolent signal in the probed representation and amplified benevolent attribution at report.

candidates.title: LADS: Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling of Tool Results for Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Web agents complete multi-step online tasks through repeated browser actions and model calls. Their returned observations lie on the critical path to subsequent decisions. When concurrent browser actions finish in bursts, observations can accumulate on a constrained return path to a shared inference service, while waiting histories compete for reusable cache state. Conventional delivery rules prioritize short transfers or immediate cache reuse but overlook how sending a result earlier can help a request resume sooner and free cache-protection capacity for other waiting requests. We present LADS (Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling), a tool-result scheduler that couples cache-aware delivery with bounded prefix leases. Its key insight is that resumption lets extra protection references retire, making lease quota available to protect another waiting history. LADS prioritizes timely handoffs using current lease ownership and an estimated resumption delay, with bounded departures from Cache-first order. Compared with ReAct using first-in, first-out (FIFO) tool-result delivery, LADS reduces mean complete-workflow latency by 44.6% under bursty tool returns and by 42.4% on Web-derived burst replay.

candidates.title: Automated Database Schema Matching Using Agentic Large Language Models and Semantic Similarity
candidates.abstract: Automated database schema matching is an essential process for integrating heterogeneous databases and enabling consistent data exchange across diverse information systems. Traditional schema matching techniques rely on linguistic, structural, instance-based, and machine learning (ML) approaches, but they often struggle with inconsistent naming conventions, domain-specific terminology, complex relationships, and evolving data structures. New developments in large-scale language models allow for better semantic reasoning and contextual comprehension, which in turn improves the ability to find relationships between database attributes. However, standalone models may produce inconsistent predictions and require additional validation for reliable matching. This paper reviews automated database schema matching using agentic large language models and semantic similarity techniques. It examines fundamental schema matching methods, semantic similarity approaches, automation strategies, and agentic reasoning capabilities, including planning, search, and tool utilization. Existing frameworks, including LLM-Matcher and Matchmaker, are discussed alongside machine learning, multimodal fusion, and explainable matching approaches. The review identifies research gaps in autonomous decision-making, iterative validation, scalability, explainability, and reduced human intervention. Finally, it highlights the need for an integrated framework combining agentic reasoning and semantic similarity to achieve accurate, adaptive, transparent, and efficient schema matching across heterogeneous database environments.

candidates.title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
candidates.abstract: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking

candidates.title: A Survey on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-PDF Question Answering Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively separates knowledge retrieval from generation for private document question answering. This study explores the design space of document-grounded QA and details a multi-PDF RAG system. The pipeline uses PyMuPDF for text extraction with OCR fallback, BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 for dense embeddings, and ChromaDB for storage. Semantically similar chunks are retrieved via cosine distance to generate answers using a local Llama 3.2:3B model via Ollama. Built with React/Vite and FastAPI, the system supports document management and query APIs. The paper reviews RAG methodologies—including hybrid retrieval, reranking, and GraphRAG—while maintaining a local, modular architecture optimized for consumer-grade hardware. Finally, it evaluates the system's strengths and limitations to identify future research directions.

Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite is selected for its low-latency, cost-efficient characteristics, operating with a 1,048,576-token input limitand 65,536-token output limit. candidates.title: Context-Shielded Backdoor Attack against Large Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) routinely use inference-time visual-token compression to prune hundreds of patch tokens down to a compact budget. Existing LVLM backdoors fire whenever a triggered image appears, whereas prior deployment-triggered attacks activate only when model weights are quantized or pruned. However, conventional LVLM backdoors exhibit nearly 100% attack success rate (ASR) under full-token inference, immediately exposing compromised checkpoints during pre-deployment auditing. We reveal context stripping: surrounding clean visual tokens suppress an embedded trigger at full length, whereas token pruning strips this context away and activates the backdoor. Motivated by this finding, we propose StripWake, a projector-only backdoor that remains dormant under full-token auditing yet activates across unseen compressors. Specifically, StripWake pairs clean-supervised full-token views with target-supervised randomized compressed views, and aligns early visual attention with a frozen benign teacher to preserve clean utility. On LLaVA-1.5-7B across nine unseen compressors, StripWake stays dormant at 0.4% full-token ASR yet achieves 94.0%-99.7% compressed ASR across five primary compressors without CIDEr loss.

candidates.title: The Blind Spots of Detection: Adversarial Perturbation Attacks against Watchdogs in Distributed LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Decentralizing large language model (LLM) inference across untrusted Web nodes requires robust verification to ensure computational integrity. Existing activation-based verification and detection mechanisms validate intermediate outputs against reference values, permitting bounded numerical deviations to accommodate benign cross-hardware discrepancies. However, a critical security question remains: what can a malicious worker achieve while operating within these tolerance bounds? In this work, we introduce Hush-Up, a stealthy availability attack against distributed LLM inference, where a single malicious worker halts generation while evading attribution. The attacker first profiles its local execution to model an empirical bound of benign hardware errors. Using this error bound as a feasibility constraint, the attacker optimizes an adversarial perturbation on its output activations to maximize the final-layer probability of the end-of-sequence (EOS) token, i.e., to hush up the model. Across diverse models and benchmarks, Hush-Up effectively forces premature generation termination and collapses model capabilities. Furthermore, the attack hushes up the watchdogs themselves: existing defenses often fail to detect the sabotage entirely or falsely attribute the amplified downstream anomalies to honest workers. Our findings expose a fundamental gap between local numerical verification and end-to-end accountability: perturbations too small to indict a worker locally can nevertheless be powerful enough to break distributed inference globally.

candidates.title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

candidates.title: RTP-LLM: Building an Evolvable and Reliable LLM Inference Engine at Alibaba Scale
candidates.abstract: Large language models and inference techniques evolve rapidly, making model enablement a recurring production task rather than a one-time integration effort. At Alibaba, a shared inference infrastructure must keep pace with new models and serving capabilities while remaining reliable across heterogeneous production environments. To reconcile rapid evolution with production reliability, we present RTP-LLM, an open-source production inference engine developed and deployed at Alibaba. Its architecture separates model-specific execution from shared request processing, state management, and resource coordination. Explicit interfaces localize compatible model changes while allowing models and deployment configurations to reuse common serving mechanisms. RTP-LLM has evolved from an exploratory system into a shared production engine that supports $\sim$100 models and processes hundreds of trillions of tokens per day. We describe how its architecture and production practices accommodate model evolution and contain the impact of failures, and share lessons for building evolvable and reliable inference engines at enterprise scale.

candidates.title: EMASFL: Ensemble of Multi-Agent Small Language Models for Local Fault Localization
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) have significantly advanced Fault Localization (FL) in software debugging but face challenges regarding data privacy, high API costs, and latency. While Small Language Models (SLM) offer a fast, secure, local alternative, they typically lack the reasoning capabilities required for autonomous software repository exploration. This paper proposes EMASFL, a novel local FL system integrating multi-agent architecture with ensemble method. EMASFL overcomes SLM limitations by decomposing the debugging process into a four-step structured workflow executed by specialized agents. The system employs a hybrid strategy, assigning distinct SLM to agents based on their specific strengths in following instructions or code understanding, and integrates outputs from diverse agent configurations using an ensemble method. Evaluations on the Defects4J benchmark demonstrate that EMASFL significantly outperforms existing SLM-based and traditional FL techniques. Notably, it correctly localized 169 bugs, surpassing commercial LLM-based approaches utilizing GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o mini. Operating with an average runtime of 93 seconds and zero API costs, EMASFL provides a practical, high-performance, and privacy-preserving solution for automated software debugging.

candidates.title: Do Orthogonality Constraints Help Language-Model Training Beyond Sphere Optimization?
candidates.abstract: A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every $d$ rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size $d$ is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no $d>1$ used throughout the network reliably outperforms $d=1$, and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At $d=1$, the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.

candidates.title: Stateful Monitor-Router-Rollback Regulation for Robust Functional Recovery in Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Prompt injection can divert large language model (LLM) agents from authorized objectives and contaminate subsequent conversational context. We investigate a deterministic Monitor-Router-Rollback (MRR) supervisory controller designed to detect suspicious instructions, constrain execution paths, and reconstruct trusted task context after exposure. The evaluation uses 400 matched attack scenarios, four attack families, three locally served models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 32B, and Mistral-Nemo 12B), seven completed defense conditions, and four recorded phases yielding 33,600 completed model-scenario-defense-phase observations. Our findings demonstrate model-dependent robustness improvements—particularly for Llama 3.1 8B, where automated utility increases from 36.00% to 81.25% under MRR—while establishing rigorous methodological boundaries regarding semantic adjudication, component attribution, and repeated snapshot reconstruction.

candidates.title: Research on Adaptive Workflow Orchestration Mechanism for Large Language Model Agents with Dynamic Task Graphs and Budget Constraints
candidates.abstract: To address the problems of insufficient adaptability of fixed processes, failure cascading, and uncontrolled resource consumption in long-chain tasks for large language model agents, this paper proposes a state-aware adaptive orchestration mechanism based on dynamic task graphs and budget constraints.This mechanism combines task difficulty, execution history, remaining budget, quality confidence and risk exposure into a single state vector, and then selects a workflow based on the combined utility of quality, cost, latency and risk.Runtime re-orchestration is performed by online reliability updates, partial rollbacks and verification gates.Secondary statistics from publicly available data on WebArena and automated agent design research show that the overall success rate of fixed agents in real-world long-chain environments is significantly lower than that of manual operations.Workflows obtained through automated search also outperform representative manual processes in the four task categories of reading, mathematics, multi-task and science.This study shows that the orchestration object should change from a fixed role sequence to an observable, evaluable and rollback-capable dynamic task graph, and provides a way to build stable and cost-effective agent systems.

candidates.title: A Review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Architectural Evolution, Key Breakthroughs, and Vertical-Domain Practices
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on massive pretraining based on the Transformer architecture and show significant emergent effects in general tasks. However, the nature of their statically parameterized knowledge causes vertical-domain applications to face three core bottlenecks: knowledge hallucination, delayed timeliness, and loss in long contexts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) realizes the decoupling of computational logic and factual memory through the paradigm of “retrieve first and generate afterward”. It can dynamically inject domain knowledge without fine-tuning and has become a mainstream technical path for the implementation of trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI). This study systematically reviews the evolution of RAG technology from 2024 to 2026, from Naive RAG to Advanced RAG, Modular RAG, and graph-enhanced RAG. It analyzes in depth the breakthrough progress of four key technologies, namely hybrid retrieval, multimodal document parsing, generation control, and lightweight deployment. Combined with typical application cases in complex equipment manufacturing, energy and power, public services, and other fields, it explains the engineering value of RAG. Finally, it discusses the evaluation system, existing limitations, and future trends, providing a reference for academic research and practical implementation of RAG technology.
